content.text:
# Hartwell Supply Co.: what you're looking at

Hartwell is a family-held HVAC/R distributor: about 150 people, twelve branches (Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Dayton, Toledo, Akron, Indianapolis, Fort Wayne, Louisville, Lexington, Troy MI and Pittsburgh), selling equipment, parts, refrigerant and supplies to heating and cooling contractors. The records run from 2016 to 2025.

**Its systems, each a separate database copied into the warehouse:**
- **ERP** (`erp_*`): customers and their account managers, the sales reps, products and vendors, sales orders and their lines (how each order arrived and who keyed it), purchase orders, transfers between branches, and returns.
- **Warehouse management** (`wms_*`): every stock movement (opening balances, receipts, sales, transfers, returns) and goods receipts. Stock on hand isn't stored anywhere: it's the running total of the movements.
- **Accounting** (`finance_*`): invoices and their lines, credit memos, customer payments, vendor bills and their lines, and vendor payments.
- **CRM** (`crm_*`): calls and emails to customer service, as logged by whoever took them; and the reps' quotes, with each quote's lines, its outcome (won, lost or expired), a loss reason when the rep entered one, and the order a won quote became.
- **External** (`external_*`): real monthly heating and cooling degree days and residential building permits for each branch's county.

**Days.** `day` is an operating day, about 21 a month; `dim_date` gives the calendar date.

**What isn't here:** profitability by customer, rep or branch; why a return happened; whether an order was keyed correctly; whether a vendor bill was right. Like any real business, those have to be worked out from the records, and some of them can't be.

input.sql:
WITH b AS (SELECT fb.*, row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY po_id ORDER BY day, bill_id) rk FROM finance_vendor_bills fb WHERE po_id IN (SELECT po_id FROM finance_vendor_bills GROUP BY po_id HAVING count(*)>1)),
p AS (SELECT bill_id, sum(amount) pamt FROM finance_vendor_payments GROUP BY bill_id),
x AS (SELECT b2.day, b1.amount amt, coalesce(p1.pamt,0)+coalesce(p2.pamt,0)-b1.amount over_amt, p2.bill_id IS NOT NULL paid2 FROM b b1 JOIN b b2 ON b1.po_id=b2.po_id AND b1.rk=1 AND b2.rk=2 LEFT JOIN p p1 ON p1.bill_id=b1.bill_id LEFT JOIN p p2 ON p2.bill_id=b2.bill_id)
SELECT (SELECT max(day) FROM dim_date) last_day, (SELECT min(date) FROM dim_date) first_date, (SELECT max(date) FROM dim_date) last_date,
 sum(paid2::int) paid_seconds, round(sum(CASE WHEN paid2 THEN over_amt END),2) net_overpaid, round(sum(CASE WHEN paid2 THEN over_amt END)/10,2) net_per_year,
 sum((paid2 AND day>2479)::int) paid_not_matured
FROM x

In no case does received qty equal two bills' qty, so the copy isn't a second delivery. Hartwell pays ordinary bills exactly on vendor terms (one lag per terms class). Every ordinary bill from 2016 to 2024 was paid. Of the 1,413 '-R' bills that had come due, 962 were paid (0.6808) and 451 (1,442,763.69) were held. 15 more (21,759.97) were not yet due at the end of the data. Counting all 963 paid seconds, 1 of which falls in the final 41 days, the net overpayment is 2,727,183.80, or 272,718.38 a year over 10 years. That is after allowing for 29 pairs where the first bill had been short-paid, so 5,102.58 of those second payments covered an unpaid balance. The paid rate is flat across amount bands (0.667-0.691), PO type (0.681 for both stock and special) and branch (chi-square 17.25 on 11 df, n=1,413, within chance). Vendor shares of duplicate dollars track vendor shares of all billing: the largest vendor has 0.3796 of paid duplicate dollars against 0.3761 of all billed dollars. Neither vendor credits (6.96% vs 6.94% chance) nor offsetting later short-payments (0.1308 vs 0.1331 chance) show recovery above chance. Interpretation (not observed): something in payables stops about a third of these copies, and the records don't show what or why.  ],

(2) Held vs pending: the old '466 held' becomes 451 matured held (1,442,763.69) plus 15 not yet due (21,759.97), based on the terms-fixed payment lags (q162, q184). (3) The low 2025 rate is partly an end-of-data effect (0.6423 matured, q170). (4) The largest vendor's 38% reflects its share of billing (0.3796 vs 0.3761, q167), so I reworded the next step. (5) Branch differences are within chance (q168). I added the challenger's supporting tests: single-day receipts equal to PO qty (q178), no offset recovery (q165), and no payment-record anomalies (q150, q175). I lowered confidence that the money is unrecovered to medium, because bank and statement data are absent. Nothing in the challenge needed rebutting.",
 "accepted": true
}

content.text:
I accepted all of the challenge and saved the revised finding as `finding.json`. It still stands, just with tighter numbers. I didn't need to rebut any part of the challenge. I ran one check of my own (q209) and it matched the challenger's figures.

**What changed:**
- **Size:** I now count net overpayment instead of gross. In 29 pairs the first bill had been only partly paid, so 5,102.58 of those second payments went toward a balance that was actually owed. That brings the total to **2,727,183.80, or 272,718.38 a year** over 2016–2025 (q148, q170, q209).
- **Held vs. not yet due:** Hartwell pays every ordinary bill exactly on the vendor's terms. So of the 466 unpaid '-R' copies, 451 (1,442,763.69) were actually held, and 15 (21,759.97) just hadn't come due when the data ends. Of the 1,413 copies that had come due, 962 were paid (0.6808) (q162, q184).
- **2025:** its lower paid rate is partly because the data stops at year end. On bills that had come due, 2025's rate is 0.6423 (n=137) (q170).
- **Largest vendor:** its 38% of the duplicate dollars matches its 37.6% share of all billing (q167). It's a starting point for reconciliation because the money is concentrated there, not because it behaves differently.
- **Branches:** the differences in held rate are within chance (chi-square 17.25 on 11 degrees of freedom, n=1,413) (q168).

**Supporting evidence I added from the challenge:**
- None of the 944 stock orders shows a second delivery: each was received on a single day, and the quantity received equals the order quantity (q178).
- There's no sign of the money coming back through later deductions from vendor bills. The match rate (0.1308) is the same as for ordinary bills (0.1331) (q165).
- The payment records themselves look clean: no orphan, zero or negative payments, and no reused invoice numbers (q150, q175).

**Confidence:** high that these copies were recorded as paid, but now only medium that the money is still unrecovered. There's no bank or vendor statement data to check whether vendors refunded or offset any of it. I added a next step: review the 15 copies that aren't due yet before they get paid.
